overview.title: Why build(): automatic shape inference vs NaiveDense
overview.chapter: 3 Introduction to TensorFlow, PyTorch, JAX, and Keras
overview.subsection: 3.6.2 Layers: The building blocks of deep learning
overview.main_topic: How Keras layers infer input shapes, the burden of explicit input sizes in chapter 2's NaiveDense, and the base Layer.__call__() that builds on first call
overview.central_idea: Keras layers infer their input shape from the first inputs they see. Chapter 2's NaiveDense needed input_size in its constructor, which forces every layer to know the previous layer's output size. Keras moves weight creation into build(input_shape), which the base __call__ runs automatically once before delegating to call(). The four-layer model then needs only output sizes.
overview.importance: This page gives the actual reason for the build()/call() split in Listing 3.33. It is a core design idea of Keras and is needed for writing custom layers correctly.
learning_objectives: Explain why passing input sizes explicitly to constructors is fragile
Read the schematic Layer.__call__() and trace when build() and call() run

prerequisites: Calling layers and the Sequential example (p.118)

summary:
Following the Sequential example on p.118, the page notes that **the layers received no information about their input shapes**. They **inferred their input shape as the shape of the first inputs they see**.

**The alternative is worse.** Chapter 2's toy `NaiveDense` needed the input size passed to its constructor so it could create its weights. A model then looks like

`NaiveSequential([NaiveDense(input_size=784, output_size=32, "relu"), NaiveDense(32→64, "relu"), NaiveDense(64→32, "relu"), NaiveDense(32→10, "softmax")])`,

where every layer must be told the previous layer's output size. It gets worse when a layer's output shape follows a complex rule, such as `(batch, input_size * 2 if input_size % 2 == 0 else input_size * 3)`. Then you would have to work that rule out by hand for the next layer.

**The Keras solution.** Reimplementing NaiveDense with automatic shape inference gives exactly `SimpleDense` with its `build()` and `call()` methods. Weights are no longer created in the constructor but in a dedicated state-creation method, `build()`, which receives **the first input shape seen by the layer**. `build()` runs automatically the first time the layer is called through `__call__()`. That is why the computation lives in a separate `call()` instead of in `__call__()` directly. Schematically, the base layer's `__call__` is:

```
if not self.built:
    self.build(inputs.shape)
    self.built = True
return self.call(inputs)
```

With automatic shape inference, the earlier model becomes `keras.Sequential([SimpleDense(32, activation="relu"), SimpleDense(64, activation="relu"), SimpleDense(32, activation="relu"), …])`, giving only output sizes. The listing continues on p.120.

concepts.name: Automatic shape inference
concepts.definition: Layers infer their input shape as the shape of the first inputs they see, and create weights accordingly.
concepts.intuition: Each brick measures the brick below it when they are first snapped together.
concepts.technical: Implemented by Layer.__call__: if not built, build(inputs.shape) and set built = True; then return call(inputs).
concepts.significance: It removes duplicated size information and avoids hand-computing complex output shapes.
concepts.example: keras.Sequential([SimpleDense(32), SimpleDense(64), …]) needs no input sizes.
concepts.misconception: Shape inference doesn't let a built layer accept inputs of any size. After the first build, the non-batch input dimensions are fixed by the weights.

concepts.name: Layer.__call__ / build / call contract
concepts.definition: Calling a layer runs the base __call__, which builds the layer once from the input shape and then runs call().
concepts.intuition: __call__ is a receptionist that makes sure your room (weights) is ready before sending you to the meeting (computation).
concepts.technical: `def __call__(self, inputs): if not self.built: self.build(inputs.shape); self.built = True; return self.call(inputs)` (schematic, per the book).
concepts.significance: It explains where to put code in custom layers.
concepts.example: SimpleDense(32)(x) builds W from x.shape on the first call.
concepts.misconception: The real __call__ does more than this schematic: eager/graph routing and masking (p.120).

concepts.name: Sequential model
concepts.definition: A Keras model that is a linear stack of layers mapping a single input to a single output.
concepts.intuition: It is a conveyor belt of layers.
concepts.technical: keras.Sequential([...layers]) applies the layers in order; each infers its input shape from its predecessor's output.
concepts.significance: It is the simplest way to build models in Keras.
concepts.misconception: Sequential can't express branches or multiple inputs; those need the Functional API or subclassing (p.120).

deeper.title: Weight shapes resolved by inference
deeper.body:
For the NaiveSequential widths, assuming the final 10-unit softmax layer appears on p.120 as in the naive version:

| Layer | W | b | params |
|---|---|---|---|
| 784→32 | (784, 32) | (32,) | 25,120 |
| 32→64 | (32, 64) | (64,) | 2,112 |
| 64→32 | (64, 32) | (32,) | 2,080 |
| 32→10 | (32, 10) | (10,) | 330 |

The total is **29,642**. In the Keras version, only the second column's *column* counts are written by you; the row counts come from inference. (Our computation.)

deeper.title: Explicit sizes vs inference
deeper.body: Explicit sizes (NaiveDense) let you create weights immediately and inspect them before any data arrives. Inference (Keras) defers that until the first call. Beyond the book: Keras also lets you build early when you need to, e.g. by giving the model an `Input` shape or calling `model.build(input_shape)`, so you get the benefits of both.

deeper.title: Measuring analogy
deeper.body: NaiveDense is like ordering curtains by typing in the window's width yourself, for every window, in order. SimpleDense is a curtain that measures the window when you first hang it.

misconceptions.claim: build() must be called manually before using a layer.
misconceptions.correction: The base __call__ calls it automatically the first time the layer is called.

misconceptions.claim: Putting the forward pass directly in __call__ is equivalent.
misconceptions.correction: It would bypass the automatic build step; that is why the book uses a separate call().

misconceptions.claim: Shape inference means each Keras layer guesses its shape from its constructor arguments.
misconceptions.correction: It uses the shape of the first actual input it receives.

misconceptions.claim: The schematic __call__ is the full implementation.
misconceptions.correction: It's schematic. The real one also handles eager/graph routing and masking (p.120).

takeaways: Keras layers infer their input shape from the first input they see.
Explicit input sizes (NaiveDense) duplicate information and break when widths change or output-shape rules are complex.
build(input_shape) creates weights; the base __call__ runs it once, sets built = True, then calls call().
Put the forward pass in call(), not __call__().
With inference, models specify only output widths: Sequential([SimpleDense(32), SimpleDense(64), …]).

questions.question: In the schematic __call__, what happens on the second call to a layer?
options: build() and call() both run again
Neither runs; the cached output is returned
questions.explanation: After the first call self.built is True, so the build branch is skipped and call(inputs) runs. Weights are not rebuilt, and outputs are not cached.

questions.question: Why was NaiveDense's design (input_size in the constructor) not ideal?
questions.answer: Each layer must be told the previous layer's output shape, which duplicates information and is error-prone, especially when output-shape rules are complex.
questions.explanation: From the NaiveSequential paragraph and the complex-rule example.

questions.question: A hypothetical layer outputs (batch, input_size * 2 if input_size % 2 == 0 else input_size * 3). If it receives input_size 64 and then feeds a NaiveDense, what input_size must that NaiveDense be given? And for input_size 33?
questions.explanation: 64 is even, so ×2; 33 is odd, so ×3. With shape inference you would not need to compute this.

questions.question: Why does Keras define the computation in call() rather than directly in __call__()?
questions.answer: Because __call__ is the base class's entry point that first runs build() (once, with the input shape) and then delegates to call(). Overriding __call__ would skip automatic weight creation.
questions.explanation: The page states this directly: 'that's why we defined the computation in a separate call() method rather than in the __call__() method directly!'

questions.question: What argument does build() receive?
options: The first input shape seen by the layer
questions.answer: The first input shape seen by the layer
questions.explanation: build() receives the first input shape (inputs.shape in __call__). Units come from the constructor, and neither the previous layer nor the loss is passed.

questions.question: For the NaiveSequential model, how many parameters does the 32 → 64 layer have?
questions.explanation: A dense layer has input_size × output_size weights plus output_size biases.

questions.question: Can you explain, without looking, the four lines of the schematic __call__ and what would go wrong if self.built = True were omitted?
questions.answer: Without the flag, build() would run on every call, recreating (re-initializing) the weights each time, so the layer could never keep learned values.
questions.explanation: A self-check of the lazy-build mechanism.
